sentences.text: Revenue, net interest income plus noninterest income, rose from $96.6 billion in FY2016 to $182 billion in FY2025, a 12.3% three-year CAGR to FY2025 [D5][D206][D335].
The path was a step change rather than a smooth compound: revenue was $121.6 billion in FY2021 and $158 billion in FY2023, a 30.0% jump in two years [D110][D159].
Net interest income drove that step, rising 33.8% in FY2023 as higher rates expanded deposit margins, with Payments revenue up 22% on deposit margin expansion [D174][P37].
FY2025 growth slowed to 2.8%, with net interest income up 3.1% and noninterest income up 2.4% [D226][D221][D222].
North America supplied 76.6% of FY2025 revenue but only 0.2pp of its growth, while EMEA and Asia-Pacific each added 1.2pp [D249][D251][D276][D301].

Noninterest income's 2.4% FY2025 rise reflected higher Markets revenue, asset management fees and a $588 million First Republic-related gain, offset by the absence of the $7.9 billion Visa gain in FY2024 [D222][P27].
Net interest income's 3.1% gain came from higher Markets net interest income and Card revolving balances, largely offset by deposit margin compression and lower rates [D221][P28].
Operating costs grew 1.4pp slower than revenue in FY2025, at 4.2% [D225][D226].
EPS grew 1.4% against a 2.6% net income decline as the diluted share count fell 3.4% [D216][D214][D224].
The efficiency ratio was 52.4% in FY2025, below the 57.2% window median and above the 51.7% window low [D207][D333][D331].
Noninterest expense rose 4.2% on higher compensation, brokerage and distribution fees, auto lease depreciation and technology and marketing investment [D225][P26].
The credit-loss provision reached 7.8% of revenue in FY2025, above the 6.0% peer median and the 5.6% FY2016 level [D208][D341][D7].
Net margin of 31.2% sat 21.2pp below the 52.4% efficiency ratio's complement, with the 21.4% effective tax rate and the provision the main gaps [D210][D207][D203][D208].
Operating cash flow was -$147.8 billion in FY2025 against $57.0 billion of net income, a -2.59x conversion [F60][F30][D204].
The outflow came from higher trading assets, securities borrowed, loan originations and other assets, partly offset by net income and higher trading liabilities [P21].
Operating cash flow has been negative in three of the last five years, so it is not a meaningful earnings-quality measure for this bank [F59][F60][F55].
Capital return instead: buybacks plus dividends of $48.2 billion in FY2025 against $57.0 billion of net income [D205][F30].
Return on average equity was 16.1% in FY2025, at the 100th percentile of the seven-bank peer group against an 11.8% median [D213][D338][D339].
Loans were 57.3% of deposits, up from 43.1% in FY2021 as deposit growth outran lending in the pandemic years [D211][D115].
Loans rose $121.1 billion in FY2025, driven by CIB Markets and AWM securities-based lending on higher client demand [P4].
Buybacks of $31.6 billion and dividends of $16.6 billion were funded alongside a $269.5 billion financing inflow, and the diluted share count fell 3.4% [X102][X112][F80][D224].
Net income for FY2021 through FY2025 in the table comes from the proxy's pay-versus-performance table, not the 10-K, differing by up to 0.10% [R1][F26][X16][F30][X20].
The gap is immaterial to ratios but the 10-K figures should be cited where precision matters [R1].
The credit-loss provision rose to 7.8% of revenue in FY2025 from 6.0% in FY2024, with criticized exposure up to $48.5 billion from $44.7 billion [D208][D185][P2].
Criticized exposure at 3.4% of wholesale credit exposure is a modest but rising credit-quality pressure to monitor [P2].
Whether the efficiency ratio holds below the 57.2% window median in the FY2026 10-K [D333].
Whether the credit-loss provision stays above the 6.0% peer median in the FY2026 10-K [D341].
Whether net interest income growth recovers above the 3.1% FY2025 rate in the FY2026 10-K [D221].
